evidence_collection_order_applied: Python, C++, Rust, Go, Java, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, Zig, Quidra (global_rules.evidence_collection_order). Quidra was examined last. The two reading decisions recorded under frozen_interpretations_fixed_before_quidra were written down before any Quidra evidence was inspected.

frozen_interpretations_fixed_before_quid.T1_reading: T1's operative text is 'a command that builds a multi-file project without hand-written per-file compiler invocations'. Unlike V1 of Build / Test Integration, T1 does NOT require a declarative manifest and does NOT exclude naming an entry source file. A single toolchain invocation that compiles two or more modules therefore satisfies T1. This reading was fixed before Quidra was examined and is applied identically to all ten languages; under it all ten satisfy T1, and T1 is non-discriminating for this metric. Where a language also has a dedicated manifest-driven driver (cmake, cargo, go build, zig build, swift build, Gradle/Maven), that stronger tool is recorded as well.
frozen_interpretations_fixed_before_quid.task_scoping_of_clause_c: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test clause (c) admits a tool that the official implementation repository's CI invokes. Read without a scope this would admit any tool any CI happens to run (pip in llvm-project's CI, cmake and ctest in quidra's CI, golangci-lint in microsoft/TypeScript's CI), which would make T1-T6 vacuous for every language. The scoping rule applied uniformly here is: the tool must perform the indicator's named task ON SOURCE OF THE LANGUAGE BEING SCORED. Consequences recorded before Quidra was examined: golangci-lint (Go linter in microsoft/TypeScript CI) is NOT counted for TypeScript; pip (in llvm-project CI) is NOT counted for C++. The same rule later excluded cmake/ctest/clang-format (which build and check the C++ compiler sources in quidra's own CI) from counting for Quidra.
frozen_interpretations_fixed_before_quid.T3_reading: T3 requires 'a linter or static analyzer that reports issues beyond the compiler's or interpreter's default error set'. A tool qualifies when its documented purpose is static analysis or linting distinct from compilation, whether it is a separate binary (clang-tidy, jdeps, clippy, go vet, detekt, eslint, swift-format lint) or a documented distinct analysis mode of the toolchain driver (clang --analyze invokes the Clang Static Analyzer, documented as its own tool). Merely enabling additional compiler warning options (javac -Xlint, tsc --strict, clang -Weverything) does NOT qualify, for any language. This was fixed before Quidra was examined and is why Zig's 'zig ast-check' (documented as 'Look for simple compile errors') does not satisfy T3.

T2 code formatter: `quidra fmt FILE.qui [--check]` rewrites source into canonical form; verified by rewriting a deliberately misformatted file. Clause (a). State S5.
T6 package/dependency manager: `quidra package install|lock|remove|list|path` executed on the host. Clause (a). State S5.
criteria_failed: T3 linter/static analyzer: no admissible tool. `quidra check` is the compiler's own type checker (the default error set), not analysis beyond it; the CLI has no lint subcommand and the repository ships no Quidra linter. cmake/ctest/clang-format appear in quidra's CI but operate on the compiler's C++ sources, not on Quidra source, and are excluded by the task-scoping rule applied identically to TypeScript and C++.

T4 test runner: no admissible command that DISCOVERS and executes tests. Quidra provides a test CONSTRUCT (the `test` standard namespace: `test.check`, `test.equal`, failed assertion exits status 1), but there is no `quidra test` subcommand and no discovery mechanism; `quidra run FILE.qui` executes one named file. The repository's own tests/ directory is driven by shell scripts and C++ gtest against the compiler, not by a Quidra test runner.

T5 API documentation generator: no admissible tool. The CLI has no doc subcommand. `quidra describe` emits a machine-readable summary of the LANGUAGE, not documentation of a program's declarations; `quidra inspect` emits typed source nodes as JSON. Neither produces API documentation from source declarations and doc comments.

cross_language_consistency_note: The same six indicators, the same three-clause admissibility test, and the same five host-availability states were applied to all ten languages, and the level was then computed mechanically from (T, H) with no holistic step. Three readings that the rubric text leaves open were fixed in writing BEFORE Quidra was examined and applied identically to every language: (1) T1 requires only a single command that builds a multi-file project, not a manifest - under it all ten satisfy T1, so T1 discriminates nothing here; (2) clause (c) admits a CI-invoked tool only when that tool performs the indicator's task on source of the language being scored - this excluded golangci-lint for TypeScript, pip for C++, and later cmake/ctest/clang-format for Quidra, all for the same reason; (3) T3 requires a tool whose documented purpose is analysis distinct from compilation, so extra compiler warning flags never satisfy it for any language - this is why Zig's ast-check fails T3 and why clang --analyze (the separately documented Clang Static Analyzer) passes it for C++. Cross-check of the ten assignments: the five 100s (Python, C++, Rust, Go, Swift) all have T=6 with at least four tools executed here; the four 80s (Java, TypeScript, Kotlin, Zig) split into two distinct routes that the rubric scores identically, T=5 (Java, TypeScript, Zig) and T=6 with H<=3 (Kotlin), and this was verified not to be an inconsistency but the rubric's own 80-level definition; Quidra alone has T=3. No two languages with the same satisfied-indicator profile received different levels. Host presence was established the same way everywhere - the tool's documented version or help command executed on the frozen host - and absence was classified by reason, not by bare failure, so Kotlin's five absent tools and C++'s two absent tools are recorded as S3 rather than being confused with a missing capability. Every indicator scored NOT SATISFIED was classified as S1 (the capability does not exist) rather than S3, in exactly four places: Quidra T3/T4/T5, Java T2, TypeScript T5 and Zig T3.
limitations: C++ T6 is the single most contestable admission in this metric. C++ has no package manager published by WG21 or the LLVM Project. vcpkg and Conan were considered and NOT admitted: Microsoft is not in C++'s frozen official_project_set (only WG21, the LLVM Project and Apple are), no page under llvm.org, clang.llvm.org or developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode that was examined names either tool, and llvm-project's CI invokes neither. T6 was instead satisfied by Swift Package Manager under clause (b), on an Apple Xcode documentation page inside C++'s frozen official_docs_root that names C++ explicitly, and verified on this host by building a C++ target from a Package.swift manifest. An auditor who rejects that admission records C++ at T=5 and score 80.

Java T6 rests on a single clause-(b) sentence in Oracle's JDK 26 migration guide ('If you use Maven or Gradle to build your application...'). That is inside Java's frozen official_docs_root, but it is the only naming of Maven found there; openjdk.org pages for jtreg, JMH, JMC, Skara and the Developers' Guide were checked and either returned HTTP 403 to this host or contained no Maven/Gradle mention. If the sentence were rejected, Java would fall to T=4 and score 60 - a result the frozen document's own tool_admissibility_test.why argues against, since it names 'Maven, Gradle and JUnit for Java' as tools the three-clause test exists to admit.

Python T2 and T3 rest on clause (c) via python/cpython's .pre-commit-config.yaml (ruff-check, ruff-format), which .github/workflows/lint.yml executes through a pre-commit runner rather than invoking ruff directly, plus .github/workflows/mypy.yml as corroboration for T3. No clause (b) naming of a linter was found on typescriptlang.org/docs or /tools. If rejected, TypeScript falls to T=4 and score 60.
